**Short answer:** It's not forbidden, but it needs approval. Friday deploys are outside the normal deploy window and require sign-off from the on-call engineering manager [1][2].

- **Normal window:** Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [1][2].
- **Friday:** Allowed only with approval from the on-call engineering manager [1][2].
- **Rollbacks:** Always allowed, at any time, without approval, including during freezes [1][2][3].

**Other things to check before a Friday deploy:**

- **Longer rollout:** Canary bake time is now 45 minutes, up from 20. A typical non-data-plane change takes about 50 minutes to reach all cells after merge [2].
- **Data-plane waves:** Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` roll out in waves, with 30 minutes between each. They take about two and a half hours to reach every cell [2].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** No normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd [3]. Today is Saturday, October 31, which is after the October 30 last business day, so this freeze is likely in effect until invoices go out in early November. Check with the billing team before touching Ledger [3][4].
- **Approvals for sensitive changes:** Schema migrations, infrastructure config, retention changes, and auth or billing logic need change-approver sign-off, and Restricted services also need Security sign-off [3].

Note that the October 2026 pipeline note says it updates the handbook's Deploys section, and the handbook will be edited to match. Where they differ, the note takes precedence [2]. I did not find a document that changes the Friday rule itself.

A patient qualifies for the sliding-fee program if household income is **under 250% of the federal poverty level** [1]. Once approved, it reduces visit costs by **40–100%** [1]. The sources don't say how the discount is set within that range, so staff would need to confirm that with the billing team.

Other points for this patient:

- Front desk staff can start the application at check-in [1].
- Patients in the program get the sliding-fee discount on vaccines and injectables, which are otherwise priced at cost plus administration. The 20% prompt-pay discount doesn't apply to those [2].
- Fees for records requests are waived for sliding-fee patients [3].
- No patient is denied care because of inability to pay [1].

For reference, the self-pay visit rates are $165 for a new patient, $120 for an established patient, and $79 for telehealth [1]. Those are the starting point before any sliding-fee reduction.

Critical lab results must reach the ordering clinician within **60 minutes**. If that clinician can't be reached within **30 minutes**, the result goes to the on-call medical director [1]. Each notification must be documented in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

To reach the on-call medical director, call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. The service pages the on-call medical director and pages the backup if there's no callback within 10 minutes [2]. Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers, because pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [2].

A related rule: a critical lab value called in by the reference lab is a separate trigger. It requires notifying the supervising physician within 30 minutes [1].

Emergency access to a customer workspace lasts **2 hours**, and a second engineer must approve it [1].

**Approval steps**
1. Run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>`. Every request must reference an open support case or declared incident [1].
2. A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation approves the request in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [1].
3. Access is read-only by default. Write access, such as editing a pipeline for the customer, needs the customer's written consent in the case first [1].

**Duration**
The 2-hour window is deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [1][4]. If you need more time, submit a new request with an update on the case [1].

rows.answer:
No, you shouldn't do that. Removing the name doesn't make the history safe to paste into a chatbot.

- **Removing the name isn't enough.** Halcyon's policy says "de-identified" is not a loophole, so any patient details should be treated as protected health information (PHI) [1].
- **Public chatbots are not approved.** General-purpose AI assistants on any device, including personal phones, are on the not-approved list [1]. The HIPAA policy also prohibits putting PHI into AI tools that aren't on the approved list [4].
- **The internal assistant is off-limits for patient details too.** Halcyon Assist answers policy questions only, and staff should not paste patient details into it, even without names [1].

**What you can use:**
- **Quillon Ambient** (AI scribe) is approved for PHI, but only at the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics, with patient verbal consent at each visit and clinician review of every note [1][2].
- **Meridian draft replies** can draft patient portal responses inside the EHR, but a clinician must edit or approve them before they are sent [1].

If you need a summary, use the EHR's own tools. If you think a different AI tool would help, the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) must review it first. That needs a security risk assessment, a signed business associate agreement, an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a clinical safety review. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks [1].

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's chart over three days (July 21–23, 2026) at the Riverside and Northgate clinics [1].

**Why it happened**

The root cause analysis identified three contributing causes [1]:

- **Unannounced feed change:** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, without notice [1].
- **Weak fallback matching:** The interface engine could no longer find the MRN, so on July 21 it fell back to a rule that matched results on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
- **No monitoring:** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule [1].
- **No contractual notice requirement:** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

**Detection and impact**

A medical assistant at Riverside noticed on July 23 that a potassium result didn't match the patient's history. The feed was stopped and the MRN mapping was corrected before restoration on July 24 [1]. Two patients had abnormal results routed to another chart, and their follow-up was delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].

**Corrective actions**

- Removed the name-and-birth-year fallback, so unmatched results go to a manual queue (done Sept 15) [1].
- Added an alert when more than 1% of results from any lab use a fallback match in an hour (done Sept 30) [1].
- Amending the lab agreement to require 30 days' notice of feed changes (in progress, due Dec 31) [1].
- Adding a positive patient identification check before results reach the patient portal (in progress, due Nov 30) [1].

Halcyon doesn't use a five-business-day postmortem window. Its closest equivalent is a **root cause analysis (RCA) completed within 45 calendar days** of the event becoming known. Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets an RCA, and QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours [1].

Other time limits in the same policy:

- **Within 1 hour:** For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1].
- **Immediately:** Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport [1].
- **Within 72 hours:** QPS charters the RCA team [1].
- **Within 45 calendar days:** The RCA is completed [1].

The policy doesn't give a separate postmortem deadline. It also doesn't say how "really serious" maps to Level 1 or Level 2, so check the event level with QPS. Completed RCAs go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe, which meets monthly [1]. Privacy breaches follow a separate process under the HIPAA privacy policy [1].

Halcyon needs a **signed business associate agreement (BAA)** before any patient data goes to a vendor, and a **security risk assessment** completed before go-live. Those are the two requirements that matter most for your question.

**What's required**

- **Signed BAA before any PHI is disclosed.** Under the HIPAA privacy policy, a vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate. The BAA must be signed first, and that includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [1].
- **Security risk assessment.** Any tool that will handle PHI needs one [2][4].
- **Entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.** New systems that hold PHI need an entry before go-live. The HIPAA Security Officer maintains the list [4].
- **Clinical safety review by the CMIO, for clinical use.** This applies to AI tools used in clinical care [2].

**How this plays out in practice**

- Quillon Ambient (AI scribe) has an executed BAA dated July 30, 2026, and a completed security risk assessment from July 2026. Its BAA prohibits training on Halcyon data [3].
- Tallgrass Survey Co. has a passed security assessment but no executed BAA. Halcyon has no PHI sharing with them until the BAA is signed. The open issue is data retention: Tallgrass wants 5 years and Halcyon will accept 18 months [1].

**Who to contact:** The Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) handle these requests [2]. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2].

I didn't find the full HIPAA privacy policy in the knowledge base, so the requirements above come from the vendor records, the AI tools policy, and the systems inventory. Check the policy text itself before relying on this as the complete standard.

Northwind has a close equivalent, but it's built for a different situation. Its "emergency access" lets support and on-call engineers into a customer's workspace, not clinical records. Northwind is a software company, so the two policies cover different kinds of access.

**Halcyon (break-the-glass, Meridian EHR)**
- A clinician opens a chart outside their normal patient relationship, picks a reason, and types a justification. No one approves it in the moment [1].
- Access lasts until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [1].
- Every event is reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days, and the manager is asked to confirm unclear reasons [1].
- Misuse is a privacy incident and can lead to termination [1].

**Northwind (emergency access to customer workspaces)**
- An engineer must reference an open support case or declared incident ID. "Curiosity" and "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [2].
- A second engineer from support or on-call must approve the request in Teleport before access starts. The approver can't be the requester or on the same case [2].
- Access is read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case first [2].
- Access expires after 2 hours, which is shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [2][4].
- Sessions are recorded and kept for one year. The customer's audit log shows the access, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security samples sessions weekly, and reviews every session that used write access [2].

**Main differences**
- **Approval:** Halcyon's is self-service with after-the-fact review. Northwind requires a second person's approval up front.
- **Trigger:** Halcyon's is a patient-care need. Northwind's is a documented support case or incident.
- **Duration:** Halcyon allows up to 12 hours. Northwind allows 2 hours.
- **Customer visibility:** Northwind notifies the customer. Halcyon's policy doesn't mention patient notification.

**No, not for the sensitive categories at either company.** The rules differ in how broad they are.

**Northwind Labs:** Restricted data, which includes customer event payloads, credentials, and encryption keys, must never be in Slack [1]. The same goes for customer payloads in support replies: use field names and counts instead [4]. Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is not banned from Slack outright. It is shared only on a need-to-know basis [1]. If you see unexpected data, such as another customer's data, stop and report it in `#security-help` right away [4].

rows.answer:
You need two sign-offs, plus an ADR.

1. **PLAT's change approver.** Archived events live in Driftwood, which PLAT owns [4]. Lifecycle rule changes are normal changes, and normal changes need sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the service [1][3].
2. **Head of Security or the security on-call delegate.** Driftwood stores Restricted data [4], and normal changes to Restricted services also need security sign-off [1]. You request `@northwind/security` on the PR [1].

Other requirements:

- **ADR:** Any change that alters how long customer data is kept needs an ADR, linked from the PR [1].
- **PR process:** Add the `change:normal` label, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [1]. Approvals expire after 7 days, so re-request if the change hasn't shipped by then [1].
- **Customer notice:** If you shorten retention for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period, the account team must give 30 days' notice [1].
- **Freezes:** Normal changes are blocked from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027 [1]. Rollbacks are always allowed [1].

The current default archive retention is 365 days, and per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [3]. Enterprise customers can contract for up to 730 days with security team approval [3].

The three cycle 5 big bets were Tributary, Lantern, and Hydrant [1].

- **Tributary**: streaming joins (the Enrich step), pitched by Mateo and LZ. The cycle scope covered CDC-backed snapshots, the editor preview, dead-letter routing, and a private beta with design partners in October. GA stays January 2027 [1]. It started private beta on October 1 with eight design partners [5].
- **Lantern**: the self-serve billing portal, pitched by NH and HV. The original target was a December beta and January 2027 GA, and it depends on the payment-provider migration [1]. The October leadership notes moved GA to March 2027 and the beta to February [5]. The codename register also lists February beta and March GA [4].
- **Hydrant**: automatic scaling for ingest gateways per cell, pitched by OA. It included the gateway TLS session ticket change from INC-2291 as a small batch item [1]. It shipped to all production cells on October 22, 2026 [3][4].

Seven pitches came in, and the handbook limits each cycle to three big bets [1][2]. Tidepool was not picked in cycle 5 and needs a re-pitch with smaller scope [4].

Northwind's default is 365 days for archived event payloads. This is the current standard, version 2.0, effective September 15, 2026, which replaced the earlier 400-day default [2].

- **Archived event payloads (Driftwood, cold store):** 365 days by default [2].
- **Hot buffer (Kafka):** 7 days [2].
- **Enterprise customers:** they can contract for longer archive retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2]. Shorter periods are also possible by contract [1].

Archive retention is enforced by object-storage lifecycle rules, with per-workspace overrides stored as bucket tags [2].

Enterprise customers can use reference tables of up to **500 million rows per workspace**, according to the streaming joins product spec [1]. That is a spec target, not a confirmed shipped limit. Tributary is in private beta, with GA targeted for January 2027 [4].

For context, the Growth plan limit is 50 million rows [1]. The snapshot design keeps each runner partition's reference state within a 2 GiB memory budget, and partitions that exceed it spill to disk rather than failing [2]. Rebuilding a 50M-row snapshot after a restart takes about 25 minutes today, which is why an RFC proposes persisted snapshots [2].

I couldn't find the renewal date for Bayline's BAA in the knowledge base. There is no business associate record for Bayline Reference Laboratories, and no document states when its BAA was executed or when it renews.

What I did find about Bayline:

This is a change to the contract, not a renewal date.

To get the date, check the executed Bayline agreement with Lab contracts or Clinical Operations, since they own the amendment work [1]. Someone could also ask the HIPAA Security Officer whether a BAA record exists for Bayline, because the vendor inventory requires one for any vendor that handles PHI [5].

A hold on the gateway count can last at most **4 hours**. The launch notes show the command as `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`, so the default example is 2 hours, but the hard cap is 4 hours, after which Hydrant takes over again [1]. You can release it early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell <cell>` [1].

Two related points from the same notes:
- Holds are standard changes and need no approval [1].
- Hydrant reverts manual changes to the replica count within 2 minutes, so don't use `nwctl scale ingest` by hand while Hydrant is running [1]. The on-call runbook still shows the old manual scaling command, which the Hydrant notes say has been replaced [1][5].

When a customer's integration exceeds its limit, the API returns **HTTP 429**, and the response includes a **`Retry-After` header** giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying [1].

- **Status code:** HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests).
- **Retry timing:** The `Retry-After` value, in seconds [1].
- **SDKs:** Northwind's SDKs honor `Retry-After` automatically and back off exponentially, so customers using them don't need to handle this themselves [1].
- **Billing:** Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].

Some details that affect what customers see:

- Limits are per workspace, not per API key, so multiple keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Requests can burst up to 2x the limit for 10 seconds before being rejected [1].
- Limits vary by plan and endpoint. For example, event ingest on the Starter plan is 100 req/s, and on Enterprise it's 10,000 req/s [1].
- If a customer calls an endpoint their plan doesn't include, they get HTTP 403, not 429 [1].
- Enterprise customers can have ingest limits raised up to 3x the default by contract. Growth customers can get temporary raises for one-off backfills of up to 72 hours, granted by the Data Plane on-call primary [1].

I didn't find a public-facing version of this page in the knowledge base to confirm the exact wording customers see, so customers using raw HTTP rather than an SDK should be pointed to the `Retry-After` header specifically.

**Naming rules:**

You need sign-off from **PLAT's change approver**. Hydrant is owned by PLAT, and each cell's floor and ceiling is part of its configuration in the PLAT infrastructure repo. Changing a ceiling is a normal change under the production change approval policy, which requires sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the affected service [1][5]. Security sign-off isn't needed because Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't a Restricted service [1].

The us-east cell currently has a gateway ceiling of 64 replicas [2].

To make the change:
- Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections of the template.
- Request review from the approver (or their delegate) as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [5].
- Approvals are valid for 7 days, so re-request if the change hasn't shipped by then [5].

I couldn't find the approver's name in the knowledge base. The engineering team directory should list them [5].

Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call when a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, because hitting the ceiling usually signals a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1]. Before raising the ceiling, it may be worth checking whether the us-east gateways are misbehaving. The `nwctl hydrant hold` command pins replica counts for up to 4 hours without approval, but it doesn't change the ceiling [1].

The $1,200-a-month plan is Growth. On Growth, the bulk endpoint `POST /v2/events/batch` allows **50 requests per second**, with each request capped at **10,000 events or 10 MB** [1][2].

- **Burst:** Short bursts up to 2x the limit (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds. Going over the limit returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].
- **Limits are per workspace**, not per API key, so all keys in the workspace share the 50 req/s budget [1].
- **Higher rates for a one-off backfill:** The DP on-call primary can grant a temporary raise for up to 72 hours on any plan that has the endpoint [1]. Growth limits are otherwise fixed by contract, so a permanent increase would mean talking to sales about Enterprise [1].

At the maximum size, a year of history could be sent in batches of 10,000 events, at up to 50 requests per second [1].

Three endpoints are completely unavailable on Starter. Calls to them return HTTP 403 rather than a rate-limit error [1]:

- `POST /v2/events/batch`, used for bulk backfill and replays [1]
- `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh`, used to force an Enrich snapshot rebuild [1]
- `GET /v2/audit-log/export`, the audit log CSV export [1]

The SCIM endpoints (`/v2/scim/*`) are also marked "Not available" on Starter, but they are not available on Growth either. Only Enterprise has them [1].

Starter can use the other endpoints, with lower rate limits. For example, `POST /v2/events` is allowed at 100 req/s [1]. Starter workspaces also have no overage billing, and the plan includes 5 million events a month [2].

Five production services are classed as Restricted in the service catalog [1]:

- **`ingest-gateway`**: accepts events from customer SDKs and the HTTP API, and writes them to Kafka. It keeps only in-flight payloads [1].
- **`runner`**: executes customer pipelines. It holds partition state in local RocksDB and reference-table snapshots [1].
- **Conduit**: source and destination connectors. It holds encrypted connector credentials and sync cursors [1].
- **Driftwood**: the long-term object archive behind the hot buffer, holding archived event payloads [1]. Some older runbooks call it the "cold store" [1].
- **Keystone**: authentication and authorization. It holds hashed API keys, SSO/SAML configuration and session tokens [1].

The Restricted class covers customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys, and these services must never leave production [2]. Changes to any of them need Head of Security sign-off in addition to the owning team's approval [3].

**The Regional sales director approves it**, after the deal desk reviews the quote. Under the current matrix, an Enterprise discount over 15% and up to 25% goes to the Regional sales director, and the deal desk review is required [1].

How it works:
1. Build the quote in the CRM with the discount on the first-year line.
2. Because 22% is over 15%, the quote routes to the deal desk automatically. Priscilla Okoye's sales operations team checks margin, payment terms and non-standard clauses, then forwards it to the approver [1].
3. The Regional sales director records the decision in the CRM. Email and Slack approvals don't count [1].

Target turnaround is 1 business day [1]. Approvals are valid for 30 days, and a quote that changes by more than 2 percentage points needs fresh approval [1].

The older Pricing and discount policy would send 22% to the VP of Sales, since it sets 20–30% at that level [2]. The sales desk memo from October 1, 2026 replaces that table, so the Regional sales director is the correct approver today [1].

A deploy sits in the canary cell for **45 minutes** before it can be promoted automatically. The handbook still says 20 minutes, but the October 2026 pipeline change note overrides it and says the handbook will be updated [1][2].

Promotion requires all of these during the bake:

- Error rate and p95 latency stay within 10% of baseline (unchanged) [1].
- Zero sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary [1].
- Runner consumer lag does not grow by more than 2 minutes [1].

The change was made because INC-2291 showed some failures only appear after caches or sessions expire [1].

If something looks wrong, anyone can run `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack to keep the deploy in canary. You can check progress with `nwctl deploy status` [1]. Data-plane changes (`ingest/` or `runner/`) then roll out in waves with 30 minutes between each, which affects how long they take to reach every cell [1].

No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand. The runbook step is outdated. Hydrant, the ingest gateway autoscaler, has been enabled in us-west since October 15, and it treats the replica count as its own. A manual change gets reverted within 2 minutes [2].

What to do instead:

- **Check the cause first.** The runbook says to find the affected cell on the ingest dashboard and check gateway TLS handshake errors, since brokers can look healthy while the failure is on the client side [1][3]. The dashboard has a TLS handshake errors panel [3].
- **Pin the count only if you need to.** For example, while debugging a bad gateway build, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds last at most 4 hours, need no approval, and can be released early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell <cell>` [2].
- **Watch the ceiling.** If us-west sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because that usually points to a gateway problem rather than real traffic [2].

Also, if you're in a SEV-1 or SEV-2 situation, declare it with `/incident declare` in Slack [1].

Archived events in the attic (Driftwood, the long-term event archive) are kept for **365 days** by default [2][4]. After that, object-storage lifecycle rules delete them. Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2].

The older v1 standard set the default at 400 days [1]. v2, dated September 15, 2026, replaced it [2]. Enterprise customers can contract for a shorter archive period, or a longer one of up to 730 days with security team approval [1][2].

Enterprise workspaces can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild **once every 2 minutes** through `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh`. Growth allows one per 10 minutes, and Starter doesn't have the endpoint at all (it returns HTTP 403) [1].

Some related points:

- Rate limits apply per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share the same budget. Exceeding the limit returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].
- A forced refresh discards the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it with a full table scan, which is expensive for large tables. The source notes most customers never need it, because snapshots are normally kept current with change data capture [1].

**No, don't throw the vaccines out.** Label them, keep them refrigerated, and call the clinical pharmacist. The pharmacist decides whether the stock can be used.

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use," keep it refrigerated in a working unit, and record the reading, the time, and how long the fridge has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers whether the stock is still usable [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** Use a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine was given. Use a higher level if a patient received affected vaccine [1][2].
4. **Don't give any vaccine from the affected stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Vaccine fridges must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C, so 10 °C is out of range [1]. The policy doesn't say how to reach the pharmacist on a weekend, so check your clinic's after-hours contact list. If the pharmacist can't be reached, keep the stock labeled and unused and escalate to your clinic manager or the on-call medical director.

**Not same-day, unless Elmhurst already has the vaccine on hand.** Elmhurst isn't a hub clinic, and the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) is a Tier 2 item, which means only hub clinics stock it [1][2].

To get it to Elmhurst:
- Elmhurst requests a transfer from the nearest hub. Transfers arrive within 2 business days [1].
- The hubs are Riverside, Northgate and Harbor Point [2]. The sources don't say which is nearest to Elmhurst.
- Today is Saturday, and Elmhurst's Saturday hours end at 12:00 [2]. The earliest transfer would likely arrive Tuesday, November 3, if requested today, though I haven't confirmed that.

Other requirements:
- RZV is for patients aged 50 and over. It's a 2-dose series, with the second dose 2–6 months after the first [1].
- The self-pay price is $205 per dose, and the 20% prompt-pay discount doesn't apply to vaccines [1].
- RZV can be given by an RN or clinician [1].

If the patient wants it sooner, they could be booked at a hub clinic. Riverside is open Saturday until 12:00, and Harbor Point until 16:00 [2].

Riverbend should be scheduling **1.5 medical assistants per clinician**, which means rounding up to whole people. [1]

**Bayline must respond within 30 minutes.** A stopped results feed is a P1 because it is a patient-safety risk, and Bayline's contractual first response for P1 is 30 minutes. Bayline's interface desk is staffed 24/7 [2]. That response is the time for a qualified engineer to first respond, not a time to fix the problem [2].

**On the Halcyon side, the Service Desk pages the owning team.** Bayline's owning team is INT, the interface team. The Service Desk (extension 4357, or the intranet tile) should get a ticket for every problem. For a P1, it also pages the owning team's system steward, and it tracks Bayline's response against the matrix. Clinic staff should not call Bayline directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [2].

I did not find a named INT steward in the knowledge base. The matrix says stewards are listed in the clinical systems change control policy, which I did not retrieve [2]. The on-call medical director is not the page for a feed outage. That role covers critical lab results that the ordering clinician can't be reached about, and other clinical escalations [3][4].

Four formulary items are Tier 3, meaning they aren't stocked at any clinic and must be ordered from the wholesaler for a named patient, which takes about 5 business days [1]:

- **Td** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe, $46). Tdap is preferred, and Td is given only on request [1].

- **HPV vaccine, 9-valent** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe, $295 per dose). For ages 9–45 [1].
- **Meningococcal B vaccine** (0.5 mL prefilled syringe, $190 per dose). For ages 16–23 or on specialist advice [1].

Tier 2 items (RZV, hepatitis B, ceftriaxone) are not in this group. They are stocked only at hub clinics, and other clinics request a transfer, which arrives within 2 business days [1][2].

Halcyon Health does not charge patients for a missed appointment. The no-show fee was eliminated by the revised policy, effective October 5, 2026 [2]. Under that policy, a missed appointment counts as a no-show only if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead, and cancelling by replying to a reminder counts [2].

Two related points:

- **Older fee still on record:** The 2025 policy charged a $25 fee after the second no-show in 12 months, and it was not billed to Medicaid or sliding-fee patients [1]. That policy has been replaced in full [2].
- **Unpaid old fees:** Any no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 that are still unpaid are waived. Revenue Cycle Management reverses them on statements, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [2].

No. Under the current staffing standard, every clinic, including small clinics, must have at least one RN on site during open hours. Saturday sessions also need an RN [1]. The standard took effect September 1, 2026, and replaces the 2025 version, which did not require an RN at small clinics [1][2].

For a small clinic (under 40 average visits per day), the minimum on-site coverage is:

- 1 physician or NP
- 1 RN
- 1 MA per clinician
- 2 front desk staff [1]

If coverage drops below the minimum, the clinic manager contacts the float pool first. If the clinic still can't meet the minimum, in-person visits can be converted to telehealth where clinically appropriate [1][4]. The 2025 standard also required the manager to ask the regional medical director about reducing the schedule, and to log any session run below minimum [2]. The knowledge base has no support-ticket response time for Tallgrass Survey, and the reason is that they aren't a live vendor yet. Yes. Halcyon doesn't call it a buddy, but every new clinical hire is paired with a preceptor for 90 days [1]. Northwind's onboarding buddy is a short, first-two-weeks role, so the Halcyon arrangement is much longer [2].

How the Halcyon preceptor program works:

- **Duration:** 90 days [1].
- **Check-ins:** weekly for the first month, then every other week [1].
- **Sign-offs:** the preceptor signs off on the competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [1].
- **First week:** days 4–5 are shadowing at the home clinic with the preceptor [1].

Clinicians also need active licenses, DEA registration where applicable, and verified board certification before they can see patients. Credentialing takes 30 to 60 days, so start dates are set accordingly [1].

Northwind's closest equivalent is the **service catalog**. It lists each production service, what data it stores, a data classification, and the owning team. The page is maintained by the Platform team [2].

- **What it tracks:** service name, purpose, stored data, and a data class of Restricted, Confidential, or Internal [2].
- **Who owns it:** the page says it is maintained by Platform (PLAT) [2]. Owners are listed by team code, and the engineering team directory maps each code to a manager and change approver [5].
- **How changes are made:** to change an owner, open a PR against the catalog and tag both the old and new engineering managers [2]. A new datastore needs an ADR before it appears in the catalog [2].

The catalog doesn't use the term PHI, and I found nothing in Northwind's documents that marks systems as holding protected health information. Its Restricted class is the closest analogue. Restricted covers services such as the ingest gateway, runner, and Conduit, which handle customer event payloads and connector credentials [2]. Northwind's cell inventory also lists the infrastructure cells, and it is maintained by Platform [1].

labels.text: Northwind's closest equivalent is the service catalog.
It lists each production service, what data it stores, a data classification, and the owning team.
The page is maintained by the Platform team.
What it tracks: service name, purpose, stored data, and a data class of Restricted, Confidential, or Internal.
Who owns it: the page says it is maintained by Platform (PLAT).
Owners are listed by team code, and the engineering team directory maps each code to a manager and change approver.
How changes are made: to change an owner, open a PR against the catalog and tag both the old and new engineering managers.
A new datastore needs an ADR before it appears in the catalog.
The catalog doesn't use the term PHI, and I found nothing in Northwind's documents that marks systems as holding protected health information.
Its Restricted class is the closest analogue.
Restricted covers services such as the ingest gateway, runner, and Conduit, which handle customer event payloads and connector credentials.
Northwind's cell inventory also lists the infrastructure cells, and it is maintained by Platform.

At Halcyon, patient safety events are logged in **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy says reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**Who does what**
- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed. Tell the charge nurse on shift, or the clinic manager if there is no charge nurse [1].
- **Charge nurse:** Coordinates the immediate response, assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications, or records [1]. In large clinics the charge nurse is designated; in medium and small clinics one is designated when two or more RNs are on shift, otherwise the clinic manager fills the role [2].
- **Sentinel events:** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1]. Pages go through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [3].
- **Disclosure:** The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].
- **Filing:** Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files in SafeReport [1].

**How soon**
- The policy section covering these steps is titled "Within 24 hours," but the text I found doesn't state an explicit SafeReport filing deadline. Confirm the exact filing window with QPS or the policy owner.
- Level 1 and Level 2 events get a root cause analysis. QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].

Separately, a suspected privacy incident (such as a misdirected fax or lost device) goes to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours, not through SafeReport [4].

Northwind uses a **blameless** postmortem approach, which is close to just culture but not the same thing. The docs don't use the term "just culture" and don't describe a graded framework for distinguishing human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior. Northwind's stated principle is that postmortems "look at the system and the process, not at individuals," and names appear only in the timeline [1].

**Who writes it:**
- The incident commander picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure [1].
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 needs a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [1][2].
- Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [1][2].

In practice, the INC-2291 SEV-1 postmortem lists Priya Raman as author, "with the ingest team," even though the incident commander was Oluwaseun Adeyemi [3][4]. So the author is not always the IC.

If you're comparing against your own RCA process, the main gaps to check are whether Northwind's process includes a distinction between human error and reckless behavior, and whether the author is chosen by the IC or by a separate process.

Sources:
[1] Northwind Engineering: Incident roles FAQ
[2] Northwind Engineering: On-call runbook
[3] Northwind Engineering: Northwind incident log, July–October 2026
[4] Northwind Engineering: Postmortem for INC-2291

Northwind does run periodic access reviews, and unconfirmed access is revoked automatically. But the Northwind policy covers Northwind's own production and customer-data access, not EHR access. If your compliance team is at Halcyon, the relevant documents are Halcyon's.

**Northwind Labs:** Its information security policy says quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead, and access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [3]. So if nobody signs off, the access goes away rather than staying open. The policy also says exceptions need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [3].

**Halcyon Health:** The HIPAA privacy policy says the compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection, and unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [1]. It also says clinical-system access is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1]. I found no Halcyon document that describes a periodic "does this person still need this access" recertification for Meridian EHR, or what happens if no one signs off. The monthly log review is a monitoring control, not an access recertification. If you need that control, it's worth checking with the Privacy Officer or Security Officer, since it may exist outside this knowledge base.

rows.answer:
The two organizations have different rules, and the Northwind knowledge base doesn't say how long a `#vendor-review` takes.

**Halcyon Health (patient data, AI tools)**

Halcyon staff can't put PHI into an AI tool unless it is on the approved list. Any tool that will handle PHI needs [1]:
1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement (BAA) with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

Requests go to the Privacy Officer and the HIPAA Security Officer. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [1]. Halcyon also says "de-identified" doesn't count as a loophole, so treat any patient details as PHI [1].

**Northwind Labs (customer data, `#vendor-review`)**

- Any software that will process customer data must go through the security review in `#vendor-review` before use. Subscriptions under $50/month without customer data only need manager approval [3].
- The knowledge base doesn't give a typical turnaround for this review.
- Northwind's vendor register shows what a completed review typically produces: a signed Data Processing Agreement, a review ticket number (for example, VR-41 for Parcelwise), and a record of data class and residency [4][12]. Vendors without a signed DPA can run under a security exception, as Hollowpine does [8].

If you tell me the vendor and the data it will touch, I can check the register for similar vendors. For a turnaround estimate, ask the Security team or whoever owns `#vendor-review`.

The equivalent at Halcyon is the **system steward** for the owning team. The Halcyon app is owned by Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), whose steward is **Felix Brandt** [7][1]. Bill pay is a feature of the Halcyon app [7].

For a purely cosmetic change, his approval is enough on its own. Halcyon classes cosmetic changes as minor, and minor changes need steward approval only [1]. No clinical safety sign-off or CSCAB review is required [1].

Two conditions apply:
- **It must stay cosmetic.** Changes that affect patient-facing automation, the patient app's clinical content, medication information, orders or results routing are significant instead. Those need the steward, a CMIO clinical safety sign-off, and CSCAB review [1]. A bill-pay layout tweak shouldn't fall into that category, but if it touches anything beyond presentation, reclassify it.
- **Check the Northwind comparison carefully.** At Northwind, the change approver signs off on normal changes, and standard changes need only a normal PR review [2]. Northwind's policy doesn't define cosmetic changes, so the closest match is a standard change, not a normal one. The Halcyon steward's approval is the closest equivalent to the approver's sign-off.

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs (duplicate invoices, INC-2340):** Invoice creation is now idempotent per workspace and billing period, so a second run for the same period can't create another invoice [3][4]. The root cause was that the payment provider's webhook timed out, the retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [4]. The fix was merged and deployed on October 6, and a dry run produced zero duplicates [4]. The October 8 changelog entry lists it as internal [3]. The duplicates affected 287 workspaces, and 201 card charges were refunded [2][4].

**Halcyon Health (duplicate medication reminders, IR-0412):** Reminders now carry an idempotency key made of patient, medication, and scheduled time, so a reminder whose key already exists is never sent again [1]. The duplicates happened because a September 2 scheduler cutover ran the old and new job runners at the same time, and neither checked whether a reminder had already gone out [1]. Halcyon also added two process changes: scheduler cutovers now require a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off, and reminder messages now tell patients that if they already took a dose, they don't need to take it again [1].

The two fixes address different failure paths. Northwind's guards invoice creation for a billing period. Halcyon's guards each individual reminder, and it also added process controls for cutovers.

labels.text: Northwind Labs (duplicate invoices, INC-2340): Invoice creation is now idempotent per workspace and billing period, so a second run for the same period can't create another invoice.
The root cause was that the payment provider's webhook timed out, the retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent.
The fix was merged and deployed on October 6, and a dry run produced zero duplicates.
The October 8 changelog entry lists it as internal.
The duplicates affected 287 workspaces, and 201 card charges were refunded.

Halcyon Health (duplicate medication reminders, IR-0412): Reminders now carry an idempotency key made of patient, medication, and scheduled time, so a reminder whose key already exists is never sent again.
The duplicates happened because a September 2 scheduler cutover ran the old and new job runners at the same time, and neither checked whether a reminder had already gone out.

Halcyon also added two process changes: scheduler cutovers now require a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off, and reminder messages now tell patients that if they already took a dose, they don't need to take it again.
The two fixes address different failure paths.
Northwind's guards invoice creation for a billing period.
Halcyon's guards each individual reminder, and it also added process controls for cutovers.

**Northwind (Hollowpine Helpdesk):** The sticking point is data use. Hollowpine's DPA draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines have been with legal since August. The main open issue is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [2]. Until the DPA is signed, the vendor runs under security exception SEC-EX-117, approved August 24, 2026, and AI reply suggestions must stay disabled [2]. If the DPA is still unsigned when the exception lapses, Support Operations must renew the exception or move ticket intake back to email [2]. The contract renews January 31, 2027 [2].

**Halcyon (Tallgrass Survey Co.):** The business associate agreement is the blocker. The draft was received in August 2026 and is not executed [1]. The open issue is data retention. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable survey responses for 5 years for benchmarking, while Halcyon will accept 18 months [1]. The security risk assessment was completed in September 2026 and passed with conditions [1]. The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [1]. No PHI can be shared with Tallgrass, including for pilots, until then [1]. In the meantime, post-visit satisfaction is collected through the in-app survey in the Halcyon app [1].

**Halcyon's discount is bigger in percentage terms: 20% versus Northwind's 15%.**

- **Northwind (annual Growth prepayment):** Annual prepayment on Growth earns 15% off, equal to $12,240 per year [1][2]. Growth lists at $1,200/month [1], so the saving is about $2,160 a year. The discount is measured against first-year contract value at list price [2].
- **Halcyon (self-pay, paid in full at the visit):** Self-pay patients who pay in full that day get a 20% prompt-pay discount [6]. For example, a $165 new-patient visit would drop by $33 [6]. The discount does not apply to vaccines or injectables, which are already priced at cost plus administration [7]. Patients in the sliding-fee program get that program's discount instead [7].

These are different kinds of deals, so the dollar amounts aren't comparable. Halcyon's rate is higher, but it applies per visit, while Northwind's applies to a yearly subscription.

**Northwind Labs:** The incident commander (IC) can approve an emergency change, but only during a declared incident. The owning team's change approver then reviews it retroactively within two business days [2]. The IC can also skip the canary bake with `/deploy expedite`, which is logged in `#eng-changes` [4]. Postmortems are required for every SEV-1 and SEV-2 and are due within five business days of resolution [3].

**Halcyon Health:** The on-call medical director may approve emergency changes to clinical systems [1]. Emergency changes are made to stop ongoing patient harm, and the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews them at its next meeting [5]. To reach the on-call medical director, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2 [1].

The two organizations use different approval roles and review timelines. Northwind's review is due within two business days, while Halcyon's is "at its next meeting," which is the weekly CSCAB on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [5]. The sources don't give a fixed deadline for the Halcyon review.
